309.title: Grace and works
309.hook: Catholics and Lutherans agreed in 1999 that we're saved by grace, not by works, and good works follow
309.howItsDone: Christians across the churches describe good works, such as serving the poor, giving and caring for neighbors, as a grateful response to God's grace, and some churches mark Reformation Day on October 31 with joint Catholic–Lutheran prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, repentance: metanoia, pulling over and turning the car around. Your line was turn and be forgiven. What small thing did you turn? Day three hundred nine.

Augsburg, Germany, 1999. In the city where Lutherans had once presented their confession of faith to the emperor, leaders of the Lutheran World Federation and of the Catholic Church sit down at a table and sign a document together. For centuries, the two churches had formally condemned each other's teaching on how a person is made right with God. Wars had been fought partly over it. Families split. Now they sign a statement saying: on the heart of this question, we agree. Not on everything. But on the center. Today's word is what they agreed on.
screen: `AUGSBURG, 1999.` → `CENTURIES OF CONDEMNATION.` → `ON THE CENTER, WE AGREE.`

segments.voice: Justification is a courtroom word. To justify someone is to declare them in the right. In the Bible, the question is: how does a person come to be right with God? Paul's answer, in Ephesians, is the line we read on day two hundred eighty-nine: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." And the very next lines go on: "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works." Grace first. Then good. But James, in his letter, says bluntly: "faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone." For centuries, Protestants and Catholics heard those texts pulling in different directions. Lutherans stressed that God declares sinners righteous, as a free gift received by faith alone. Catholics stressed that God's grace truly makes a person righteous from within, and that grace works through a changed life. Each suspected the other of missing something. The Joint Declaration put the shared center like this, in summary: it is by grace alone, through faith in what Christ has done, and not by anything people have earned, that God accepts them and gives the Holy Spirit, who renews hearts and calls people to good works. Both sides agreed that the old condemnations don't apply to the teaching as the other now presents it. They still differ in how they describe some things, and some theologians on both sides objected. Since then, world bodies of Methodist, Anglican and Reformed churches have affirmed it too. The order they agreed on is simple enough to fit in a pocket. Grace comes first. Good works grow out of it, the way fruit grows on a tree that is already alive.
screen: `JUSTIFY: DECLARE IN THE RIGHT.` · `EPHESIANS 2, AND JAMES 2.` · `DECLARED RIGHT, OR MADE RIGHT?` · `1999: ON THE CENTER, AGREED.` · then, large: `CREATED IN CHRIST JESUS UNTO GOOD WORKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do a good work out of gratitude. Settle, and breathe. First, remember something you've been given that you didn't earn. Stay with it for a few breaths. Then, out of that thankfulness, not out of guilt or to prove anything, choose one good thing to do today. Something small and specific: a call, a meal, a note, a chore done for someone else. If you pray, you can thank God for grace, and offer the good work as thanks. If you don't, just let gratitude choose it. The bell holds the time.
Justification. Being made right with God. Catholics and Lutherans now agree: by grace, through faith, and good works follow.
Your line: grace first, then good. Today, do your good work, and notice whether it feels different when it comes from thanks instead of fear. Day three hundred nine.

310.title: The resurrection of the body
310.hook: not escape from the body, but bodies raised and made new
310.howItsDone: Christians say "the resurrection of the body" in the Apostles' Creed, and at funerals many churches pray in the hope of the resurrection, burying or committing the body with honor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, justification, and a table in Augsburg in 1999. Your line was grace first then good. What good thing did you do out of thanks? Day three hundred ten.

Ask most people what Christians think happens after death, and you'll probably hear something like this: your soul floats up out of your body, and goes to heaven, where it lives forever on a cloud, maybe with a harp. The body stays behind, like an old coat. It's in cartoons, greeting cards, a thousand movies. But read the creed carefully, and it says something much stranger, and much more solid. Near the very end, just before life everlasting, it says: I believe in the resurrection of the body. Not the escape of the soul. The body. Raised. Your hands, your face, your voice, somehow, made new. Today's word is that line, and it's one of the most surprising things Christians believe.
screen: `A SOUL ON A CLOUD, WITH A HARP?` → `THE CREED SAYS SOMETHING ELSE.` → `THE BODY, RAISED.`

segments.voice: In the ancient world, plenty of thinkers taught that the body was a prison for the soul, and death was a release. Early Christians knew those ideas well, and turned them down. Their hope was built on Easter. The risen Jesus wasn't a ghost. In Luke, he says: touch me and see, a spirit doesn't have flesh and bones. He eats a piece of fish in front of them. In John, he still carries the marks of the nails. And yet he's changed: he appears in locked rooms, and friends don't recognize him at first. Christians say that what happened to Jesus is a first taste of what will happen to everyone. Paul uses the picture of a seed. You plant a bare seed, and what comes up is a whole plant, connected to the seed but far more glorious. "It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption." "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body." A spiritual body doesn't mean a body made of air. It means a body fully alive with God's Spirit, no longer dying. Paul admits there's a great deal we don't know about what that will be like. The Bible's last book pictures not souls leaving the earth, but a new heaven and a new earth, and God saying: "Behold, I make all things new." That's why Christians have cared so much for bodies: burying the dead with honor, running hospitals, feeding the hungry. Many churches now allow cremation too; the hope doesn't depend on what happens to the remains. If God will raise bodies, then bodies matter now: yours, and everyone else's.
screen: `NOT A PRISON FOR THE SOUL.` · `TOUCH ME AND SEE.` · `A SEED, AND WHAT GROWS FROM IT.` · `ALL THINGS NEW, SO BODIES MATTER NOW.` · then, large: `IT IS SOWN IN CORRUPTION; IT IS RAISED IN INCORRUPTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank God for your body, if you pray, or simply be grateful for it. Settle, and breathe. Think of Paul's seed. Picture your body the way he pictured it: not a shell you'll shed, but a seed, plain and bare, with more in it than it looks. Feel one part of it that's worn or scarred or aching, the part you'd least put on display. Christians say even that is not thrown away. Then think of one body you love that is tired or ill or old, someone else's. Hold that person in mind for a few breaths. If you pray, you can give thanks for your body and theirs, and for the hope that both will be raised. The bell holds the time.
The resurrection of the body. Not the soul escaping, but bodies raised and made new, as the creed says.
screen: `THE RESURRECTION OF THE BODY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: bodies matter. Today, care for one body that isn't yours: bring a meal, make a visit, offer an arm on the stairs. Day three hundred ten.

311.title: Life everlasting
311.hook: heaven, hell, purgatory: traditions differ, but all hope in God's mercy
311.howItsDone: Christians say "and the life everlasting" at the end of the Apostles' Creed, pray at funerals in the hope of eternal life, and Catholics, with some Anglicans and Lutherans, remember the dead on All Souls' Day, November 2.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the resurrection of the body: a seed, and what grows from it. Your line was bodies matter. Whose body did you care for? Day three hundred eleven.

Norwich, England, May 1373. A woman of thirty, whose name we don't know, is so sick that her priest has been called to her bedside. He holds a crucifix before her eyes. And over the next hours, she sees a series of visions. Afterwards she recovers, and later lives as an anchoress, walled into a small room beside the church of Saint Julian, and tradition gives her its name: Julian of Norwich. She writes down what she saw. In it she asks God her hardest question: why sin, why so much pain? And the answer she hears is still quoted today. Today's word is the creed's last line, and she's our guide to it.
screen: `NORWICH, MAY 1373.` → `A WOMAN NEAR DEATH.` → `HER HARDEST QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The creed ends: and the life everlasting. In John's Gospel, the Greek is zoe aionios, literally life of the age: the life of the age to come. It's not just more time, an endless Tuesday. It's a different kind of life, God's own life, which John says can begin now. John 3:16 is about it: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life." What happens after death? Here the churches honestly differ, and it's right to say who says what. The churches speak of heaven: being with God, seeing God face to face, every tear wiped away. Church teaching also speaks of hell: the real possibility of refusing God, and being separated from God. Some understand it as endless; some Christians hope that in the end even hell may be emptied, though that hope isn't the official teaching of the large churches. Catholics speak of purgatory: a purifying after death for those on their way to God, like being made ready. Orthodox Christians pray for the dead without defining purgatory, and Protestant churches generally don't hold it. But under all of it runs one hope: God's mercy. Julian heard it this way, in the old translation of her book: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." Revelation pictures the end the same way: "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death." And this closes a part of the path: the creed, line by line, from I believe to life everlasting.
screen: `ZOE AIONIOS: LIFE OF THE AGE.` · `HEAVEN, HELL, PURGATORY.` · `THE CHURCHES DIFFER, AND SAY SO.` · `ALL SHALL BE WELL.` · then, large: `GOD SHALL WIPE AWAY ALL TEARS FROM THEIR EYES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with hope for someone. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you worry about: someone who has died, or someone living who seems lost, or maybe yourself. Don't try to decide what will happen to them. That isn't yours to settle. Just hold them in hope. Let Julian's words go round slowly: all shall be well, and all shall be well. If you pray, you can entrust them to God's mercy. If you don't, simply hold them, and hope. The bell holds the time.
Life everlasting. The creed's last line: the life of the age to come, God's own life, which Christians say mercy opens.
Your line: mercy has the last word. Today, when you're tempted to write someone off, leave the last word to mercy. Day three hundred eleven.

312.title: Not ashamed (Romans 1:1–17)
312.hook: Paul introduces himself to a church he's never met, and to the good news as power
312.howItsDone: Christians read Romans in church and in Bible studies, and some memorize Romans 1:16, "I am not ashamed of the gospel," as a statement of confidence in their faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, life everlasting, and Julian's all shall be well, the end of the creed. Your line was mercy has the last word. Who did you leave to mercy? Day three hundred twelve.

A letter to strangers is hard to write. You want them to know who you are, and you want them to like you, but you also have something important to say. How do you start? Paul faces exactly that when he writes to the Christians in Rome. He's never been there. He didn't found that church. He's heard about them, and they've heard about him, perhaps not all of it good. And this letter would go on to turn lives around: Augustine, Luther and Wesley each wrote about the part it played for them. Today we begin a new part of the path: Romans. And its first big claim is today's word.
screen: `A LETTER TO STRANGERS.` → `A CHURCH HE NEVER FOUNDED.` → `A LETTER THAT TURNED LIVES.`

segments.voice: Paul opens by telling them who he is: "Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, separated unto the gospel of God." Servant. The Greek word is doulos, a slave, someone who belongs to another. That's how he chooses to introduce himself. Then he greets them warmly: "To all that be in Rome, beloved of God, called to be saints: Grace to you and peace." Remember saints from day three hundred seven: ordinary people, set apart. Then he says he longs to visit, so that he can give them some spiritual gift. And then he catches himself, and adds, in effect: I mean, so that we can encourage each other. "that I may be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me." The great apostle, correcting himself mid-sentence, so he doesn't sound like he's coming to lecture them. Then comes the line the whole letter stands on: "For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek." Why would anyone be ashamed? Because in Rome, a crucified man was the lowest thing imaginable. The cross was the empire's punishment for slaves and rebels. And Paul says: I'm not ashamed of it. It's power. The Greek word is dynamis, where we get dynamic. Then one more line, quoted from the prophet Habakkuk, the line Luther later said set him free: "The just shall live by faith."
screen: `DOULOS: A SERVANT WHO BELONGS.` · `TO ALL IN ROME, CALLED TO BE SAINTS.` · `SO WE CAN ENCOURAGE EACH OTHER.` · `THE CROSS AS POWER: DYNAMIS.` · then, large: `FOR I AM NOT ASHAMED OF THE GOSPEL OF CHRIST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: prepare to introduce yourself kindly to someone new. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you don't know yet: a new neighbor, a new coworker, the person you always see and never speak to. Picture yourself saying hello. Notice Paul's way: say who you are, simply; greet them warmly; and let it be mutual, not you giving and them receiving, but two people encouraging each other. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name, or by face. If you don't, just picture the hello, and let it be warm. The bell holds the time.
Not ashamed. Paul's first big claim in Romans: he's not ashamed of the good news of a crucified Christ, because it is the power of God.
Your line: not ashamed. Today, introduce yourself kindly to someone new, and don't be ashamed of who you are. Day three hundred twelve.

313.title: Everyone has gone astray (Romans 1:18–3:20)
313.hook: Paul argues that Jew and Gentile alike have missed the mark
313.howItsDone: Some Christians end the day with an examination of conscience: looking back over it, naming where they fell short, and asking God's forgiveness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul introduced himself to a church in Rome he had never met, and your line was not ashamed. Did you introduce yourself kindly to someone new? Day three hundred thirteen.

A group chat, late in the evening. Someone starts listing everything wrong with everybody else. The coworker who never refills the coffee. The neighbor with the leaf blower at seven. Everyone piles on. Then one friend types a single line: you do that too. Silence. Paul does exactly this to his readers in Rome. Through the rest of his first chapter he describes a world that has turned away from God: greed, envy, gossip, cruelty, people who know better and don't care. It's easy to hear the listeners nodding. Yes. Them. And then he turns around and points at the one nodding. Today's word is the one he's building toward.
screen: `A LIST OF EVERYONE ELSE'S WRONGS.` → `THE LISTENERS NOD.` → `THEN PAUL TURNS AROUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the turn, in the King James Bible: "Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest: for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself." Whoever you are. The finger that was pointing out now points back. Paul builds his case in two halves. First, the nations who never had the law of Moses. They still had creation, he says: God's power can be seen in the things that are made. And they still had a conscience, a law written on the heart, that sometimes accuses and sometimes excuses. Second, his own people, the Jewish people, who had the law and the promises. Paul is a Jew himself, arguing as an insider, and he says having the law is a gift, but hearing it isn't the same as keeping it. Then he lands the point with a string of lines, mostly from the Psalms: "There is none righteous, no, not one." Nobody gets to stand on the balcony and look down. Now the word. In Greek, the word Paul uses for sin is hamartia. Its verb, in older Greek, could mean to miss: a spear thrown that falls short of the target. So sin, for Paul, is not only a list of bad deeds. It's a condition everyone shares, a whole aim that's off. Christians describe how deep that goes in different ways, and we'll meet those differences in the days ahead. But the text is plain on one thing: Paul isn't sorting the world into good people and bad people. He's putting everyone in the same room. And that's where the good news can start.
screen: `WHOSOEVER THOU ART THAT JUDGEST.` · `CREATION AND CONSCIENCE.` · `THE LAW, HEARD AND NOT KEPT.` · `HAMARTIA: MISSING THE MARK.` · then, large: `THERE IS NONE RIGHTEOUS, NO, NOT ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: admit one way you missed the mark. Settle, and breathe. Let yesterday play back slowly, like a video. Somewhere in it, you aimed at kindness, or patience, or honesty, and fell a little short. Don't hunt for the worst thing you've ever done. Just find one small, real miss. Name it plainly, without a speech in your own defense and without beating yourself up. Then notice: whoever you judged this week has missed too, and so have you. Same room. If you pray, you can bring that one miss to God and leave it there. The bell holds the time.
Sin. Hamartia in Greek, a word that could mean missing the mark. For Paul, not just bad deeds but a condition everyone shares.
Your line: all of us. Today, the next time you catch yourself judging someone, finish the sentence honestly: and I do that too. Day three hundred thirteen.

314.title: But now (Romans 3:21–26)
314.hook: the hinge: all have sinned, and all are justified freely by grace
314.howItsDone: Christians often learn Romans 3:23–24 by heart; Protestant preaching returns to it again and again, and Catholic and Orthodox teaching reads it alongside baptism and a lifelong healing by grace.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was sin, hamartia, missing the mark, and your line was all of us. When you caught yourself judging, did you finish the sentence: and I do that too? Day three hundred fourteen.

A door weighs far more than its hinge. The hinge is a small piece of metal, and the whole door swings on it. Paul's letter to the Romans has a hinge, and it's two words long. For more than two chapters he has been building a case that sounds like a courtroom closing argument. The nations without the law: guilty. His own people with the law: guilty too. Every mouth stopped, he says. The whole world stands in the dock. The gavel is about to come down. And then, right where the verdict should be, Paul writes two little words, and the whole letter swings open. Those two words are today.
screen: `A DOOR SWINGS ON A HINGE.` → `THE WHOLE WORLD IN THE DOCK.` → `THEN TWO LITTLE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here they are, in the King James Bible: "But now the righteousness of God without the law is manifested." But now. In Greek, nuni de. Everything before this was the bad news, laid out carefully. Everything after is the good news. And Paul doesn't take back a word of the bad news. He says it again, in a line of its own: "For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God." All. Nobody is let off. But the very next line is just as wide: "Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus." Notice the pattern. The same all who fell short are the all who are offered grace. Now three words to open. Justified comes from the courtroom. In Greek it's about being declared in the right, set right with the judge. Freely is the Greek word for a gift, something you don't pay for. It's the same word John's Gospel uses when Jesus says they hated him without a cause: for nothing. And grace, charis, means favor you didn't earn. Since the Reformation, Christians have argued about this passage, so here's who says what. Protestants in Luther's line hear justified mainly as a verdict: God declares the guilty person righteous, as a gift received by faith. Catholics and Orthodox Christians tend to stress that God's grace also makes a person righteous, healing and changing them over a lifetime. Remember the table in Augsburg from day three hundred nine: on the center, Lutherans and Catholics now say they agree. And the hinge itself is right there in the text. The story doesn't end at all have sinned. It turns on but now.
screen: `NUNI DE: BUT NOW.` · `ALL HAVE SINNED.` · `JUSTIFIED FREELY, AS A GIFT.` · `DECLARED RIGHT, OR MADE RIGHT?` · then, large: `BUT NOW THE RIGHTEOUSNESS OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say but now. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something that feels like a final verdict about you. A thing you did. A label you've carried. A sentence that begins I'm the kind of person who. Let it be there, honestly. Don't argue with it. Then, on an out-breath, say quietly: but now. Say it again on the next breath. You're not erasing what happened. You're letting the story keep going past it. If you pray, you can hold that verdict before God and leave the next line to God. The bell holds the time.
But now. Nuni de in Greek. The hinge of Romans, where the verdict of all have sinned swings open into grace.
Your line: but now. Today, when an old mistake comes back to accuse you, let it finish its sentence, then add two words of your own: but now. Day three hundred fourteen.

315.title: Abraham believed (Romans 4)
315.hook: Abraham trusted God and it was counted as righteousness
315.howItsDone: Christians often point to Abraham as the model of faith, and many pray by naming a specific worry and entrusting it to God, sometimes with the words of a psalm.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hinge of Romans, two words, and your line was but now. When an old mistake came back to accuse you, did you add those two words? Day three hundred fifteen.

Picture an old man standing outside his tent at night. He's well past seventy-five. His wife Sarah is old too, long past childbearing. They have no children, and by every sensible measure they never will. And God takes him outside and says: look up, count the stars if you can. So shall your descendants be. That's the scene in Genesis. Now picture Paul, centuries later, in the middle of his big argument about grace, and he needs one example everyone in Rome respects, Jew and Gentile alike. He doesn't pick a king or a prophet. He goes back to that old man under the stars. Today's word is what Abraham did there.
screen: `AN OLD MAN UNDER THE STARS.` → `COUNT THEM, IF YOU CAN.` → `PAUL GOES BACK TO ABRAHAM.`

segments.voice: Paul quotes Genesis, in the King James Bible: "Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness." Two words to open. First, believed. The Greek verb is from the same root as pistis, faith, and it means trust more than opinion. Abraham didn't agree to a list of ideas. He leaned his whole weight on a promise. Second, counted. That's an accountant's word in Greek: credited, entered in the ledger. Abraham's trust was written into his account as being in the right with God. Then Paul makes a sharp point about timing. In Genesis, this verse comes before Abraham is circumcised, before the covenant sign. So, Paul says, Abraham is the father of everyone who trusts like this: his own people, and the nations too. And Paul doesn't pretend it was easy. He says Abraham looked honestly at his own body, as good as dead at about a hundred, and at Sarah's, and still trusted. "Who against hope believed in hope." Genesis is honest too: Abraham and Sarah both laugh at the promise at different moments, and they try a plan of their own along the way. Faith, in this story, is not the absence of doubt. It's trusting anyway. Christians read this chapter alongside the letter of James, which also points to Abraham and says faith without works is dead. How the two fit has been argued over, sharply at the Reformation. Many Protestants today hear them as two sides of one coin; Catholic and Orthodox teaching stresses that faith and works belong together. And Jews and Muslims also honor Abraham as a father of faith. It's been a week of big words: grace, sin, but now. Today it comes down to one old man, looking up, trusting.
screen: `PISTIS: TRUST, NOT OPINION.` · `COUNTED: CREDITED TO HIS ACCOUNT.` · `BEFORE THE SIGN, FATHER OF ALL.` · `AGAINST HOPE, BELIEVED IN HOPE.` · then, large: `ABRAHAM BELIEVED GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trust God with one thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you're gripping tightly right now. A test result. A child far away. Money. A decision you keep replaying. Hold it in your mind like something in your fist. Look at it honestly, the way Abraham looked at his own old body. Then, slowly, open your hand. If you pray, you can hand that one thing to God and leave it there for the length of this sit. If you don't pray, simply loosen your grip for two minutes and notice what happens in your chest. The bell holds the time.
Faith. Pistis in Greek: trust, leaning your weight on a promise. Abraham's was counted to him as righteousness.
Your line: counted as right. Today, when you catch yourself gripping that one thing again, open your hand once more, and look up at the sky, even for a second. Day three hundred fifteen.

myth: in Genesis, Abraham never doubted or laughed at the promise
Genesis tells of Abraham and Sarah both laughing, and of a plan of their own. faith here is trusting anyway.
the Greek word for counted comes from keeping accounts
Abraham's trust was credited, entered in the ledger, as righteousness.
for Paul, faith means agreeing to a list of ideas
pistis means trust: leaning your whole weight on a promise.

fork.setup: you're old, with no children, and God says your descendants will be like the stars. you look at your own aging body. what do you do?
options: decide the promise must be a figure of speech.
look honestly at your body, and trust anyway.
wait until there's proof before trusting.
fork.reveal: Paul says Abraham considered his body as good as dead, and still "against hope believed in hope."

original.note: Greek: faith, trust, faithfulness. the same word can mean trusting and being trustworthy.

trapdoor: what you thought: faith means believing something without evidence.
what it means: Abraham trusted a promise while looking his situation in the face, and it was counted to him as righteousness.
what a scholar hears: elogisthē, counted, is bookkeeping language, and Paul's point about timing rests on Genesis 15 coming before the circumcision of Genesis 17.
